title: The 67-Metre Wooden Pagoda Earthquakes Can't Kill | China Travel Expert
description:
In 1056, carpenters in a small county town in northern China finished a tower of wood 67.31 m tall. No steel, no concrete, and no metal nails in its joints. Nine hundred and seventy years later the Sakyamuni Pagoda of Fogong Temple in Yingxian, Shanxi, is still standing — and still the tallest wooden pagoda in the world.

This is how it works, and what it has actually been through.

Three ideas keep it up: bracket sets (dougong) whose blocks rotate and slide so that friction burns off a quake's energy; two rings of columns tied into a "tube inside a tube"; and four hidden floors, packed with diagonal braces, that act as stiff belts between the flexible storeys.

And the honest part the brochures skip: the tower is leaning. A 2004 survey found it tilted 65 cm to the north-east and compressed by 88 cm, one second-floor column had leaned more than 56 cm by 2015, four repair plans drawn up in 2002 were all shelved, and the upper floors have been closed to visitors for more than ten years. Engineers still cannot agree whether to take it apart and rebuild it or correct it where it stands.

You will often read that it has survived "more than forty earthquakes". No heritage body or engineering paper gives that number, so you will not hear it here — only what the records actually say.

• Four repair plans (2002) shelved; 2024 Tsinghua AI-assisted survey; dismantle-versus-in-place debate: CGTN 2021-05-03 ; China Daily 2024-07-15
• Liang Sicheng surveyed the pagoda in 1933: Sixth Tone ; The Paper
• 1974 repairs found tooth-shaped relics and Liao-dynasty printed scriptures inside the statues: China Daily 2006-09-06 ; Wikipedia, "Pagoda of Fogong Temple"
